Stagnant agriculture, deindustrialisation, poor infrastructure, drain, low literacy. The colonial structure is the starting point of planning. Planning Commission, mixed economy, land reforms, Green Revolution, industry (IPR 1956), public sector. Achievements and the licence-permit costs. Food self-sufficiency vs inefficiency debate. 1991 crisis, LPG, WTO era, NITI replacing Planning Commission in later current affairs. Outcomes: growth, inequality, services boom, farm distress unfinished. Measurement debates, causes, policy (growth vs targeted), multidimensional poverty in later data. Link Class 9 to technical estimates. Education and health as investment. India’s education structure, still-large quality gaps, gender. Human capital vs human development. Credit (cooperatives, SHGs, NABARD), agriculture marketing, organic farming, diversification (animal husbandry, fisheries). Rural is not only crop. Workforce, self vs hired, informalisation, jobless growth worry, government as employer. Quality of jobs matters as much as count. Energy, transport, communication, health, education as infrastructure. Public–private mix, energy shortages, health as right vs commodity. Carrying capacity, pollution, Chipko to contemporary climate. Development that keeps future options open. India’s dual burden: poverty and pollution. India, Pakistan, China: growth paths, demographic transition, HDI, reforms timing. China is not a photocopyable model; institutions differ.

economy-1.title: Economic reasoning: choices, incentives and measurement

sections.heading: Begin with scarcity and alternatives
sections.text: An economic choice uses resources that could have been used elsewhere. Opportunity cost is the value of the best forgone alternative, not every possible alternative added together. Separate positive analysis of what may happen from a normative judgment about what should happen. A model simplifies reality so that a relationship can be examined; always state what is being held constant.

sections.heading: Markets need careful diagrams
sections.text: Demand describes a relationship between price and quantity demanded under specified conditions. A change in the good’s own price is a movement along a demand curve; a change in income or preferences can shift it. Supply, production costs and market structure affect the outcome too. Equilibrium is a model of compatible plans, not a guarantee of fairness or a claim that every real market instantly clears.

sections.heading: Read the numbers critically
sections.text: A percentage change needs a starting value. An average may hide variation, and correlation alone does not establish a causal mechanism. Ask how data were collected, what the unit is and which population is represented. In an answer, use the indicator that matches the question rather than inserting any available statistic. This is especially important when comparing incomes, prices and living standards.

economy-1.trap: A model’s equilibrium is not automatically a socially desirable outcome.

practice.question: Why could average income rise without improving the position of most households?
practice.answer: Large gains concentrated in a small group can raise the mean. Examine the distribution, median, employment and living costs before inferring a broad improvement.

economy-2.title: Macroeconomics: output, money and public finance

sections.heading: Keep flows and stocks separate
sections.text: National income accounts measure economic activity over a period, while a stock is measured at a point in time. GDP records production within a territory; household well-being depends on more than aggregate output. Distinguish nominal changes from changes adjusted for prices. Transfers and financial transactions do not all represent newly produced goods and services.

sections.heading: Trace monetary transmission
sections.text: Banks, borrowers, savers and payment systems connect finance to the real economy. A policy-rate change can influence market rates, credit conditions and spending, but transmission depends on balance sheets, expectations and other conditions. Inflation is a rise in a price index over time; its sources can involve demand, supply and expectations. Avoid describing every episode with one universal cause.

sections.heading: Read budgets as linked accounts
sections.text: Government receipts and spending have different categories. A deficit is a flow during a period; accumulated debt is a stock shaped by past borrowing and other changes. Borrowing can support productive investment or finance less durable expenditure, so the use of funds and future obligations both matter. Check the latest official document before quoting current fiscal numbers or policy settings.

rows: Current prices / adjusted for price change
Necessary for comparing output over time.

terms.meaning: Value of final production within an economy over a period.
Government decisions about revenue, spending and borrowing.

timeline.event: Define what is measured and over which period.
Follow effects through institutions and incentives.

economy-2.trap: Disinflation is a slower rise in prices; it is not necessarily a fall in the price level.

practice.question: Why might a lower policy rate not immediately create more investment?
practice.answer: Banks may not fully pass it on, firms may lack demand or confidence, and debt or risk can constrain borrowers. Explain the transmission chain rather than assuming a one-step relationship.

mcq: Which is normally a stock measure?
Public debt at a specified date
Debt at a date is a stock; income, production and deficits are measured over periods.

economy-3.title: Development: jobs, capabilities and structural change

sections.heading: Growth and development answer different questions
sections.text: Growth expands output, while development also concerns capabilities, distribution and structural change. A sector can produce a large share of output without employing an equally large share of workers. Examine productivity and job quality rather than assuming that any increase in GDP automatically creates sufficient secure employment. Education and health contribute both directly to well-being and indirectly to productive capacity.

sections.heading: Connect rural and urban economies
sections.text: Agricultural productivity, storage, transport, non-farm work and migration shape household opportunities. Rural development is not limited to farm output. Credit, water, skills and institutions interact; a road without a functioning market or a loan without viable demand may have limited effects. For Bihar, explain how seasonal migration and local livelihoods connect instead of treating them as completely separate systems.

sections.heading: Trade-offs and evidence
sections.text: Infrastructure and industry can generate benefits while displacing people or imposing environmental costs. Evaluate who receives gains, who bears risks and whether safeguards are effective. Global integration creates opportunities and exposure to external shocks. Use dated official data and distinguish a policy’s stated objective from evidence of its results. Avoid using one national average as a complete account of all regions.

rows: Not a complete measure of well-being.
Health and education also have intrinsic value.
Work or enterprises outside parts of formal protection and regulation
Examine movement of workers as well as output.

terms.meaning: Resources sent by a migrant to another household or place.
Development attentive to participation and distribution of benefits.

economy-3.trap: Being employed does not establish that a person has adequate income or social protection.

practice.question: How can rising agricultural productivity support development beyond agriculture?
practice.answer: It can improve incomes, release resources, create demand and supply inputs, but the outcome depends on distribution, non-farm opportunities and the ability of workers to move into productive employment.
